summary: SENTINEL AI is an onboard medical assistant prototype for long missions where Earth is minutes away and no doctor may be aboard. It compares each crew member's readings with their own versioned baseline and automatically opens an investigation when a sustained change appears, even without a symptom report, while stale or poor-quality sensor data never creates a finding. Crew members mark symptoms on a 3D anatomical model, follow picture-by-picture guides for blood-pressure, pulse-oximeter and thermometer checks, and are routed on a habitat map to the nearest ready device, with routes that change when a hatch closes. Urgent events are never downgraded, follow-ups and screenings are tracked, and messages to the flight surgeon queue over a simulated delayed link. Real NASA data (Inspiration4 crew biomarkers, ISS radiation and ISS cell studies from NASA OSDR) is shown as labelled research context. It is a research demonstration with fictional crew data, not a medical device.
details:
SENTINEL AI — Project Details

SENTINEL AI is an autonomous, offline-capable astronaut health monitoring and medical assistance system designed to reduce the medical responsibilities placed on astronauts during long-duration space missions, particularly when immediate assistance from Earth is unavailable.

What does it do, and how does it work?

SENTINEL continuously evaluates simulated astronaut health measurements against individual health baselines. Its explainable, rule-based detection engine identifies sustained changes, checks measurement quality and automatically initiates health investigations without requiring astronauts to recognise every potential problem themselves.

The system integrates several capabilities into one connected workflow:

  • Interactive 3D Anatomical Twin: Astronauts can explore a human anatomical model, identify the location of symptoms, record their severity and view relevant health information.
  • Visual Medical Procedure Coach: Provides illustrated, step-by-step guidance for blood-pressure measurements, pulse oximetry and non-contact temperature assessments. It also validates the technical quality of simulated readings.
  • Spatial Habitat Intelligence: Displays an interactive spacecraft layout, estimates an astronaut's location using simulated wireless signals, identifies suitable medical equipment and provides routes through accessible compartments.
  • Autonomous Health Investigation: Connects health observations, symptoms, equipment availability, medical assessments and follow-up activities into a persistent workflow.
  • Emergency Assistance: Prioritises urgent situations, coordinates simulated crew alerts and queues messages for ground medical support without depending on an immediate Earth connection.
  • NASA Research Integration: Incorporates real NASA datasets to provide scientific context for the health challenges associated with spaceflight.

What are the benefits and intended impact?

The primary goal is to reduce astronaut workload while improving the timeliness, accessibility and consistency of medical assessments.

Rather than expecting astronauts to continuously interpret health readings, determine which assessments are necessary, locate equipment and remember follow-up procedures, SENTINEL automates much of the monitoring and coordination process.

Its intended benefits include earlier identification of potential health changes, clearer assessment instructions for nonmedical crew members, faster access to available equipment and more reliable medical-record management.

The broader vision is to enable greater medical independence during missions to Mars and other distant destinations. Similar technology could eventually assist medical operations in remote environments on Earth, including Antarctic research stations, offshore facilities and isolated communities.

What tools and technologies were used?

SENTINEL was developed using:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Three.js, HTML, CSS and Vite for interactive interfaces, 3D anatomical visualisation and habitat navigation.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic and SQLAlchemy for health-monitoring logic, medical workflows and API services.
  • Database: SQLite for persistent local storage of health observations, investigations, procedures and follow-ups.
  • Development and testing: GitHub, OpenAPI, Pytest and Vitest for version control, integration and automated testing.
  • AI development tools: OpenAI Codex for frontend development and Anthropic Claude for backend development.
  • 3D resources: Open Anatomy 3D and BodyParts3D-based anatomical models.

The prototype uses simulated wearables, medical instruments, wireless positioning signals and spacecraft environments. No physical medical hardware is currently connected.

How were NASA datasets incorporated?

SENTINEL integrates actual numerical measurements from NASA's Open Science Data Repository and RadLab, including:

  • OSD-575: Inspiration4 human blood metabolic biomarkers.
  • OSD-656: Inspiration4 human urine inflammation biomarkers.
  • OSD-546: Human bone-marrow stem-cell gene expression during spaceflight experiments.
  • OSD-817: Human optic-nerve tissue research relevant to spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome.
  • NASA RadLab: Historical radiation measurements collected aboard the International Space Station.

These datasets help illustrate the biological and environmental challenges of spaceflight. They are kept separate from fictional astronaut health records and are not used to make individual medical diagnoses.

What makes SENTINEL creative?

SENTINEL's main innovation is integrating autonomous health monitoring, anatomical visualisation, spatial intelligence, visual medical guidance and closed-loop medical coordination into one system.

Instead of functioning as a conventional health dashboard or medical chatbot, SENTINEL connects health concerns to practical actions.

For example, the system can identify a sustained change in simulated health measurements, open an investigation, coordinate an appropriate configured assessment, find compatible equipment within the spacecraft, guide the crew member through the measurement and schedule follow-up.

Its offline-first design also addresses the communication delays and connectivity limitations of deep-space missions.

What factors were considered during development?

The project was designed around medical accessibility, astronaut workload, operational independence, limited spacecraft resources, measurement reliability, data privacy and safety.

Particular attention was given to distinguishing genuine NASA research from simulated data, handling uncertain sensor readings, explaining automated decisions, preserving medical records and ensuring urgent events are not delayed by routine workflows.

SENTINEL is currently a functional research prototype, not a clinically validated medical device. Its medical detection rules and procedures are educational demonstrations, and future deployment would require extensive medical, hardware and operational validation.

Ultimately, SENTINEL aims to make astronaut healthcare more proactive, coordinated and accessible, helping crews focus on their missions while maintaining greater awareness and control over their health.
